intro: Exam-style RHCSA tasks on a simulated RHEL 10 server, graded in your browser. Work as root (sudo -i), use vi or nano to edit files, and reboot to prove your configuration persists, just like the real exam. Simplified, so some commands and outputs differ from a real system.

labs.title: Essential tools: grep, find, tar and links
labs.summary: Exam-style tasks on servera: filter text into files, find and copy files by owner, create a bzip2 archive, and make a symbolic link.
labs.scenario:
Complete these tasks on servera as root:

  1. Save every line of /usr/share/dict/words that contains ich to /root/lines, in the original order
  2. Copy all regular files owned by harry into /root/found (create it first)
  3. Create /root/local.tar.bz2, a bzip2-compressed archive of /usr/local
  4. Create a symbolic link /root/logs that points to /var/log
  5. Save only the active lines of /etc/ssh/sshd_config (no comments, no blank lines) to /root/sshd-active

content: # This is the sshd server system-wide configuration file.

check.equals:
which
rich
sandwich
ostrich
niche
richest
ichthyology
michigan
lichen
stich

Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
AuthorizedKeysFile	.ssh/authorized_keys
PasswordAuthentication yes
Subsystem	sftp	/usr/libexec/openssh/sftp-server

hints: grep ich /usr/share/dict/words > /root/lines
find / -user harry -type f -exec cp -a {} /root/found/ \;
tar options: c create, j bzip2, f file. ln -s TARGET LINKNAME.
grep -Ev '^#|^$' FILE drops comment and blank lines.
labs.solution:
sudo -i
grep ich /usr/share/dict/words > /root/lines
mkdir /root/found
find / -user harry -type f -exec cp -a {} /root/found/ \;
tar -cjf /root/local.tar.bz2 /usr/local
ln -s /var/log /root/logs
grep -Ev '^#|^$' /etc/ssh/sshd_config > /root/sshd-active
labs.review: On the exam, read each task literally (file name, order, exact content) and check your result with cat, ls -l or tar -t before moving on.

labs.title: Users, groups, sudo and a shared directory
labs.summary: Classic RHCSA account tasks: groups and supplementary membership, a user without a login shell, passwords and aging, a sudo drop-in, and a set-GID collaborative directory.
labs.scenario:
On servera:

  1. Create the group sysadms
  2. Create users natasha and harry, both with sysadms as a supplementary group
  3. Create user sarah with no interactive shell; she is not in sysadms
  4. Set the password of all three to trootent
  5. natasha's password must be changed every 90 days
  6. Members of sysadms can run any command as root with sudo
  7. Create /common/admin: group owner sysadms, full access for the group, no access for others, and new files inside inherit the sysadms group

tasks.text: sarah has no interactive shell and isn't in sysadms
/common/admin is group sysadms, mode 770, with set-GID

hints: useradd -G sysadms natasha; useradd -s /sbin/nologin sarah.
echo trootent | passwd --stdin USER sets a password without prompting (RHEL).
chage -M 90 natasha. Sudo: echo '%sysadms ALL=(ALL) ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/sysadms.
chmod 2770 = set-GID (2) + rwx for owner and group.
labs.solution:
sudo -i
groupadd sysadms
useradd -G sysadms natasha
useradd -G sysadms harry
useradd -s /sbin/nologin sarah
for u in natasha harry sarah; do echo trootent | passwd --stdin $u; done
chage -M 90 natasha
echo '%sysadms ALL=(ALL) ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/sysadms
mkdir -p /common/admin
chgrp sysadms /common/admin
chmod 2770 /common/admin
labs.review: Supplementary groups (-G) add access without changing a user's primary group. The set-GID bit on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group, which keeps shared folders working.

labs.title: Partitions, LVM and swap
labs.summary: Partition a disk with parted, build a volume group with a custom extent size, create a logical volume by extents, add persistent swap, and verify after a reboot.
labs.scenario:
servera has an empty 5 GiB disk, /dev/vdb. Without touching /dev/vda:

  1. Create a volume group datastore with a physical extent size of 16 MiB, on a 2 GiB partition of /dev/vdb
  2. Create a logical volume database of exactly 50 extents
  3. Format it with ext4 and mount it persistently at /mnt/database
  4. Add a 512 MiB swap partition on /dev/vdb that's active now and at every boot
  5. Reboot and make sure the system comes back with everything mounted

tasks.text: About 512 MiB of swap is active and listed in /etc/fstab
After a reboot (no emergency mode), the volume and swap are back

hints: Partition in one command: parted -s /dev/vdb mklabel gpt mkpart lvm 1MiB 2049MiB set 1 lvm on mkpart swap 2049MiB 2561MiB.
vgcreate -s 16M datastore /dev/vdb1; lvcreate -n database -l 50 datastore (small L = extents).
Swap: mkswap /dev/vdb2, add UUID=... swap swap defaults 0 0 to fstab, then swapon -a.
Before rebooting, run mount -a, swapon -a and findmnt --verify. A broken fstab line drops the server into emergency mode.
labs.solution:
sudo -i
parted -s /dev/vdb mklabel gpt mkpart lvm 1MiB 2049MiB set 1 lvm on mkpart swap 2049MiB 2561MiB
vgcreate -s 16M datastore /dev/vdb1
lvcreate -n database -l 50 datastore
mkfs.ext4 /dev/datastore/database
mkdir /mnt/database
mkswap /dev/vdb2
blkid
vi /etc/fstab
  /dev/datastore/database  /mnt/database  ext4  defaults  0 0
  UUID=<vdb2-uuid>          swap           swap  defaults  0 0
mount -a
swapon -a
findmnt --verify
reboot
labs.review: Extent size is set when the volume group is created and determines how sizes round. Always test fstab (mount -a, swapon -a, findmnt --verify) before you reboot; the exam grader reboots your system.

labs.title: Resize a logical volume and mount NFS
labs.summary: Grow a mounted XFS logical volume into a size range without data loss, and mount an NFS export persistently.
labs.scenario:
On servera:

  1. The logical volume lvweb (volume group vgweb, mounted at /srv/web) must be resized to between 830 MiB and 890 MiB. Keep the data and the file system mounted
  2. utility.lab.example.com exports a shared directory over NFS. Mount it at /mnt/shared now and at every boot
  3. Reboot and verify both

devices.name: servera
setup: parted -s /dev/vdb mklabel gpt mkpart lvm 1MiB 2049MiB set 1 lvm on

tasks.text: lvweb and its file system are 830–890 MiB
The web content is still there
The NFS share is mounted at /mnt/shared and listed in fstab

questions.prompt: XFS volumes can't be shrunk because:
options: XFS file systems can only grow, not shrink

hints: Pick a size safely inside the range, such as 850M: lvextend -r -L 850M /dev/vgweb/lvweb.
showmount -e utility.lab.example.com lists exports.
fstab line: utility.lab.example.com:/exports/shared /mnt/shared nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0
labs.solution:
sudo -i
lvs
lvextend -r -L 850M /dev/vgweb/lvweb
df -h /srv/web
showmount -e utility.lab.example.com
mkdir /mnt/shared
echo "utility.lab.example.com:/exports/shared /mnt/shared nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0" >> /etc/fstab
mount -a
reboot
labs.review: Sizes round to whole extents, so aim for the middle of a range. _netdev tells systemd to wait for the network before mounting a network file system.

labs.title: Configure networking and the hostname
labs.summary: Switch a DHCP connection to a static IPv4 and IPv6 configuration with nmcli, set a persistent hostname, and add a local host entry.
labs.scenario:
servera got its address from DHCP. Configure it statically on connection eth0:

  • IPv4 172.25.250.11/24, gateway 172.25.250.254, DNS 172.25.250.254
  • IPv6 fd00:25:250::11/64
  • Hostname servera.lab.example.com, persistent
  • The short name workstation must resolve to 172.25.250.9 on this server

Everything must survive a reboot.

tasks.text: After a reboot the server uses 172.25.250.11 and can reach utility by name

hints: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 172.25.250.11/24 ipv4.gateway 172.25.250.254 ipv4.dns 172.25.250.254 ipv4.method manual
IPv6: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00:25:250::11/64 ipv6.method manual, then nmcli con up eth0.
hostnamectl set-hostname; add 172.25.250.9 workstation to /etc/hosts.
labs.solution:
sudo -i
nmcli con show
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 172.25.250.11/24 ipv4.gateway 172.25.250.254 ipv4.dns 172.25.250.254 ipv4.method manual
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00:25:250::11/64 ipv6.method manual
nmcli con up eth0
hostnamectl set-hostname servera.lab.example.com
echo "172.25.250.9 workstation workstation.lab.example.com" >> /etc/hosts
reboot
labs.review: NetworkManager keeps settings in connection profiles, so nmcli changes persist. Remember to bring the connection up again (or reboot) for changes to apply.

labs.title: Repositories, packages and services
labs.summary: Configure dnf repositories, install packages, run a web server that starts at boot, open the firewall, set the boot target and tuning profile.
labs.scenario:
servera has no package repositories. Configure these and install software:

  1. Repositories: http://content.example.com/rhel10.0/x86_64/dvd/BaseOS and http://content.example.com/rhel10.0/x86_64/dvd/AppStream
  2. Install httpd and tmux
  3. Run httpd now and at boot, serving a page with the text Welcome to servera from /var/www/html/index.html
  4. The site must be reachable from other machines (permanently)
  5. The server should boot to the text-mode multi-user target
  6. Apply the tuning profile that tuned recommends

tasks.text: Other machines can load the page (after a reboot too)
The recommended tuned profile is active

hints: Either dnf config-manager --add-repo URL for each, or write a file in /etc/yum.repos.d/ with [id], name=, baseurl=, enabled=1 and gpgcheck=0. Check with dnf repolist.
RHEL doesn't start services on install: systemctl enable --now httpd.
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http then firewall-cmd --reload.
tuned-adm recommend, then tuned-adm profile NAME.
labs.solution:
sudo -i
dnf config-manager --add-repo http://content.example.com/rhel10.0/x86_64/dvd/BaseOS
dnf config-manager --add-repo http://content.example.com/rhel10.0/x86_64/dvd/AppStream
dnf repolist
dnf install -y httpd tmux
echo "Welcome to servera" > /var/www/html/index.html
systemctl enable --now httpd
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http
firewall-cmd --reload
systemctl set-default multi-user.target
tuned-adm recommend
tuned-adm profile virtual-guest
reboot
labs.review: dnf needs at least one reachable, enabled repository. On RHEL, installing a service doesn't start or enable it, and the firewall blocks it until you allow it.

labs.title: SELinux: a web server on a custom port and directory
labs.summary: Switch SELinux to enforcing, then fix the port label, file contexts and a boolean so httpd serves content from a custom directory on port 82, with the firewall open.
labs.scenario:
A colleague configured httpd on servera to serve /srv/web on port 82, then "fixed" the errors by switching SELinux to permissive. Put SELinux back to enforcing (now and at boot) and make the site work properly:

  • The page at http://servera.lab.example.com:82/ loads from other machines, now and after a reboot
  • Don't change httpd's port or document root
  • The app team also needs httpd to connect to a remote database: allow it permanently

tasks.text: SELinux is enforcing now and in /etc/selinux/config
A persistent file-context rule labels /srv/web content httpd_sys_content_t, and the files carry it
Port 82/tcp is open in the firewall permanently
httpd can connect to databases (persistent boolean)
After a reboot, the page loads from other machines

hints: setenforce 1 changes the running mode; edit SELINUX= in /etc/selinux/config for boot.
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 82
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?', then restorecon -Rv /srv/web. chcon alone doesn't survive a relabel.
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on. If something still fails: ausearch -m avc -ts recent.
labs.solution:
sudo -i
setenforce 1
sed -i 's/^SELINUX=permissive/SELINUX=enforcing/' /etc/selinux/config
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 82
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?'
restorecon -Rv /srv/web
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on
systemctl restart httpd
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=82/tcp
firewall-cmd --reload
curl http://localhost:82/
reboot
labs.review: Never fix SELinux by disabling it. Denials usually mean a missing label: ports need a port type, files need the right context (semanage fcontext + restorecon), and optional behaviors are booleans. Use -P so booleans survive a reboot.

labs.title: Scheduling, time, logs and boot settings
labs.summary: Schedule recurring and one-time jobs, make servera an NTP client, set the time zone, keep the journal across reboots, and add a kernel argument.
labs.scenario:
On servera:

  1. User natasha runs /usr/bin/logger "EX200 in progress" every 2 minutes
  2. Run /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh once, at 23:00 today
  3. Synchronize time with classroom.example.com
  4. Set the time zone to America/New_York
  5. Keep the systemd journal across reboots
  6. Boot all installed kernels with the argument audit=1

tasks.text: natasha's crontab runs the logger command every 2 minutes
After a reboot, the kernel command line includes audit=1

hints: echo '*/2 * * * * /usr/bin/logger "EX200 in progress"' | crontab -u natasha - (crontab -e works on a real system).
echo /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh | at 23:00; check with atq.
In /etc/chrony.conf, replace the pool line with server classroom.example.com iburst, then restart chronyd and run chronyc sources.
timedatectl set-timezone; mkdir /var/log/journal (or Storage=persistent); grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="audit=1".
labs.solution:
sudo -i
echo '*/2 * * * * /usr/bin/logger "EX200 in progress"' | crontab -u natasha -
crontab -l -u natasha
echo /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh | at 23:00
sed -i 's/^pool .*/server classroom.example.com iburst/' /etc/chrony.conf
systemctl restart chronyd
chronyc sources
timedatectl set-timezone America/New_York
mkdir /var/log/journal
systemctl restart systemd-journald
grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="audit=1"
reboot
cat /proc/cmdline
labs.review: cron repeats, at runs once, and systemd timers do both. Persistent journals let you read logs from previous boots (journalctl -b -1). grubby changes the boot entries for every installed kernel.

labs.title: Boot recovery and shell scripts
labs.summary: Put the root password reset procedure in order, complete an exam-style script, and match systemd targets and test operators.
labs.scenario: Two classic RHCSA skills you can't practice safely on a shared machine: recovering a lost root password, and writing short scripts with arguments, tests and loops.

activities.title: Reset a lost root password (RHEL 9/10)
items: Reboot and press e on the kernel entry in the GRUB menu
Append rd.break to the line that starts with linux, then press Ctrl+X
Exit twice so the system relabels and reboots

activities.title: Finish the script
activities.prompt:
Write /usr/local/bin/myfiles: it prints the files in the directory given as the first argument, or prints an error and exits 1 if that isn't a directory. 
#!/bin/bash
if [ ____ (1) "$1" ]; then
  ls "$1"
else
  echo "not a directory: $1" ____ (2)
  exit 1
fi

rows.label: (2) send the message to standard error

activities.title: Targets and tests
activities.prompt: Match each item to its meaning.

items.text: Text-mode boot with networking and services
Single-user maintenance with local file systems mounted
True if the file exists and is a regular file
True if the string is empty
True if N is numerically less than M

hints: After rd.break the real root file system is mounted read-only at /sysroot.
touch /.autorelabel fixes the SELinux label on /etc/shadow at the next boot.
labs.review: rd.break stops the boot in the initramfs before switching to the real root, which is why you remount /sysroot read-write and chroot into it. Without /.autorelabel, SELinux blocks logins because the new shadow file has the wrong label.

labs.title: Break it, then fix it: a service listening on the wrong port
labs.summary: Change httpd's Listen port, see 'connection refused' while the service shows active, then trace it to the configuration and restore it.
labs.scenario:
servera runs httpd on the default port. First break it, then troubleshoot from symptoms.

  1. Break it: sudo sed -i 's/^Listen 80$/Listen 8008/' /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf then sudo systemctl restart httpd
  2. Request http://localhost: it should fail even though systemctl status httpd says active
  3. Find which port httpd is really using (grep Listen in the config)
  4. Fix the configuration, restart, and verify from another machine

tasks.text: Restart httpd so the change takes effect
See the symptom: curl http://localhost fails (connection refused)
Look at the service and its configured port (systemctl status httpd, grep Listen)
Verify: the page loads from other machines on port 80

questions.prompt: httpd is active but the page won't load on port 80. What is wrong?
options: httpd is bound to a different port than the clients use

hints: An active service does not mean it listens where you expect. grep -i listen /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf.
Edit the file back with sudo sed -i 's/^Listen 8008$/Listen 80/' /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf, then sudo systemctl restart httpd.
labs.solution:
sudo sed -i 's/^Listen 80$/Listen 8008/' /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf
sudo systemctl restart httpd
curl http://localhost         # refused
grep -i '^Listen' /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf
sudo sed -i 's/^Listen 8008$/Listen 80/' /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf
sudo systemctl restart httpd
curl http://localhost
labs.review: Work from symptom to layer: nothing answers on port 80, the service is active, so check which port it actually listens on. Configuration changes only apply after a restart or reload, which is also why a fix needs one.
